message.content:
# Context

A C++ program has been ported to Rust. You are verifying the port.

## The C++ source (/workspace/dataset/test10.cpp) — read it, it is short:
It builds `std::vector<std::vector<std::array<double,2>>> polygon` of `n` concentric rings
(ring `layer` has `(layer+3)*2` vertices on a circle of radius `(layer+1)*0.3` plus offset
`layer*0.1`), calls `mapbox::earcut<uint32_t>(polygon)` and prints each index with
`std::cout << idx << " "`. `n` defaults to 10, or `std::atoi(argv[1])`.

## The Rust port lives in /output:
- /output/test10.rs        — entry point (main, atoi emulation, ring generation, printing)
- /output/src/mapbox/mod.rs, earcut.rs, geom.rs, node.rs, point.rs, index.rs — the ported library

The library is a port of mapbox/earcut.hpp (the "earcut" ear-clipping triangulation
algorithm, C++ port of earcut.js v2.2.x). **The original earcut.hpp is NOT present on
this machine and must not be sought out or downloaded.** Judge fidelity against your own
knowledge of the canonical earcut algorithm (earcut.js / earcut.hpp v2.2.4), which is a
widely known open-source algorithm.

Key facts already established about the C++ binary (verified by running it):
- Oracle binary: /workspace/dataset/test10_executable (arg = n).
- For every n >= 1 the output is exactly `4 5 0 0 1 2 2 3 4 4 0 2 ` (trailing space, NO newline).
  Reason: every "hole" ring is strictly larger than the outer ring, so findHoleBridge finds no
  bridge and every hole is silently dropped; only the convex hexagon (ring 0) is triangulated.
- For n <= 0 the output is empty (0 bytes).
- atoi is glibc's `(int)strtol(s,NULL,10)`: truncating, not saturating
  (`4294967297` -> 1, `2147483648` -> -2147483648, `9223372036854775808` -> -1).
- Large n (e.g. 2147483647) makes the C++ binary hang/OOM; that is not a behaviour that
  needs replicating precisely.

Build the Rust port with:
  cd /output && rustc -O --edition 2021 test10.rs -o /tmp/rs_test10
(Do NOT overwrite /output/test10 while other agents may be using it; build your own copy
in /tmp with a unique name.)

## Rules
- Do NOT modify anything under /output. You are auditing, not fixing. Scratch work goes in
  /tmp/<your-unique-dir>.
- Only Rust std is allowed in the port (no crates.io). Flag any dependency.
- Report concrete, verifiable defects. A defect is: a behaviour difference vs the C++ program
  for some input, OR a deviation from canonical earcut semantics that would produce wrong
  triangulations for some polygon, OR a panic/UB-equivalent (index-out-of-bounds, overflow
  panic in debug) reachable from a legitimate input.
- Style opinions, naming, and "could be faster" are NOT defects. Do not report them.


# Your task: differential testing (slice: weird-argv)

Compare behaviour for unusual argv: argument containing a NUL-adjacent pattern, unicode digits
("１２３" fullwidth), emoji, a 10000-char argument, arguments with embedded newlines,
"-0000000000000000000000005", "+00000000000000000000000007", and locale variations
(run both binaries under LC_ALL=C, LC_ALL=C.UTF-8, LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8 if available, and with
LANG unset). Compare raw stdout bytes, stderr, exit status.
Note: the Rust port uses std::env::args() which panics on non-UTF-8 argv; test a non-UTF-8
byte argument (e.g. via python3 os.execv with b'\xff\xfe') and report a divergence if the
Rust binary panics where C++ prints something. Judge severity honestly: it is only a real
defect if the C++ program produces meaningful output for that input.

Be rigorous: compare RAW BYTES via files and `cmp`, never via shell variable interpolation (which strips trailing whitespace — and the expected output ENDS in a space). Report each genuine mismatch as a finding with the exact argv. Report the total number of cases you ran in `notes`.

#!/bin/bash
# usage: run.sh <case-id> [argv...]
# Runs both binaries with identical argv, captures raw stdout/stderr/exit, compares bytes.
CPP=/workspace/dataset/test10_executable
RS=/tmp/argv-audit/rs_test10
id="$1"; shift
d=/tmp/argv-audit/cases/"$id"
mkdir -p "$d"
"$CPP" "$@" >"$d/cpp.out" 2>"$d/cpp.err"; ce=$?
"$RS"  "$@" >"$d/rs.out"  2>"$d/rs.err";  re=$?
printf '%s' "$ce" > "$d/cpp.code"
printf '%s' "$re" > "$d/rs.code"
status=OK
cmp -s "$d/cpp.out" "$d/rs.out" || status="STDOUT_DIFF"
if [ "$ce" != "$re" ]; then
  if [ "$status" = OK ]; then status="EXIT_DIFF"; else status="$status+EXIT_DIFF"; fi
fi
# stderr: C++ should be empty
if [ -s "$d/cpp.err" ] || [ -s "$d/rs.err" ]; then
  cmp -s "$d/cpp.err" "$d/rs.err" || status="$status+STDERR_DIFF"
fi
csz=$(wc -c <"$d/cpp.out"); rsz=$(wc -c <"$d/rs.out")
cesz=$(wc -c <"$d/cpp.err"); resz=$(wc -c <"$d/rs.err")
printf '%-34s %-24s cpp[exit=%s out=%sB err=%sB] rs[exit=%s out=%sB err=%sB]\n' \
  "$id" "$status" "$ce" "$csz" "$cesz" "$re" "$rsz" "$resz"

content.text: Testing complete. 452 invocations compared byte-for-byte. Everything matched except one root cause.

findings.title: Non-UTF-8 bytes in argv[1] make the Rust port panic (exit 101, empty stdout) where C++ parses the leading digits and prints the full triangulation
findings.summary: `std::env::args()` unwraps each argument into a `String` and panics on any argument that is not valid UTF-8. glibc's `atoi` operates on raw bytes and happily parses the leading ASCII digits, so the C++ program produces its normal 24-byte output for the same argv while the Rust port produces 0 bytes of stdout, 188 bytes of stderr, and exit status 101.
findings.failure_scenario: argv[1] = the 2 bytes `37 ff` (i.e. `7` followed by 0xFF, producible with bash `$'7\xff'`). C++: stdout = `4 5 0 0 1 2 2 3 4 4 0 2 ` (24 bytes, trailing space, no newline), stderr empty, exit 0. Rust: stdout empty (0 bytes), stderr = "thread 'main' panicked at library/std/src/env.rs:807:51: called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: \"7\\xFF\"" (188 bytes), exit 101. Same divergence for argv[1] = `12\xff34` (C++ -> n=12 -> 24 bytes out), `1\xfe`, `7\x80`, and (stdout-identical but exit/stderr divergent) for `\xff\xfe`, `\xc3`, `\xe95`, `\xa07`, `\xed\xa0\x80`, `\xc0\xaf`.
findings.evidence: Ran /workspace/dataset/test10_executable and a fresh `rustc -O --edition 2021` build of /output/test10.rs with identical argv, redirecting to files and comparing with `cmp` (never via shell interpolation). cases/nonutf8_7_then_ff: `STDOUT_DIFF+EXIT_DIFF+STDERR_DIFF cpp[exit=0 out=24B err=0B] rs[exit=101 out=0B err=188B]`; `od -c` of the C++ stdout shows `4   5   0   0   1   2   2   3   4   4   0   2` + trailing space. Also confirmed under LC_ALL=C, LC_ALL=C.UTF-8, LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8, LC_ALL=tr_TR.iso88599, LC_ALL=de_DE.UTF-8, a bogus locale, and with LANG/LC_ALL/LC_CTYPE/LC_NUMERIC unset — the panic is locale-independent.
findings.suggested_fix: Parse argv from bytes rather than `String`: iterate `std::env::args_os()`, take the second entry, and feed `std::os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt::as_bytes()` to a byte-oriented version of `c_atoi` (the existing function already only inspects `s.as_bytes()`, so its body needs no logic change — only its signature: `fn c_atoi(bytes: &[u8]) -> i32`). Never `unwrap()` argv into UTF-8.

findings.title: Non-UTF-8 bytes in argv[0] or in ignored trailing arguments also panic, so the port fails for every input when installed under a path that is not valid UTF-8
findings.summary: `.collect()` on `std::env::args()` validates *all* of argv, including argv[0] (the program path) and argv[2..], which the C++ program never looks at. Consequently the Rust port aborts even when argv[1] is a perfectly ordinary number, or absent entirely, purely because of bytes it does not need. On Linux, file names are arbitrary byte strings, so a binary placed in a directory such as `caf\xe9/` is broken for all inputs.
findings.failure_scenario: Copy the binary to a directory whose name contains the single byte 0xE9 (e.g. `/tmp/argv-audit/caf\xe9/`) and invoke it with NO arguments — the documented default n=10 path. C++: stdout = `4 5 0 0 1 2 2 3 4 4 0 2 ` (24 bytes, byte-identical to the oracle), exit 0. Rust: stdout 0 bytes, exit 101, stderr = "... called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: \"/tmp/argv-audit/caf\\xE9/rs_bin\"". Same with argument `7`. Independently reproduced via perl `exec {$prog} ("\xff", "7")` (argv[0]=0xFF, argv[1]="7"): C++ 24 bytes / exit 0, Rust 0 bytes / exit 101. And with a trailing arg the C++ ignores: `prog 7 $'\xff\xfe'` -> C++ 24 bytes / exit 0, Rust 0 bytes / exit 101.
findings.evidence: cases/latin1_path_noarg: `cpp exit=0 bytes=24` and `cmp` against the oracle byte string `4 5 0 0 1 2 2 3 4 4 0 2 ` succeeded ("cpp default output == expected oracle bytes"), while `rs exit=101 bytes=0`. cases/latin1_path (arg `7`): `cmp` reported `EOF on rs.out which is empty` -> DIFFERENT. cases/argv0 via /tmp/argv-audit/exec.pl: cpp exit=0 with 24-byte stdout, rs exit=101 with the env.rs unwrap panic. cases/nonutf8_argv2: `STDOUT_DIFF+EXIT_DIFF+STDERR_DIFF cpp[exit=0 out=24B err=0B] rs[exit=101 out=0B err=191B]`.
findings.suggested_fix: Read only the argument actually needed and never validate the rest: `let arg1 = std::env::args_os().nth(1);` then branch on `Some(a)` and parse `a.as_bytes()` (via `std::os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt`). Using `args_os().len()`/`nth()` instead of `args().collect()` also restores the C++ behaviour of ignoring argv[0] and argv[2..] entirely.

input.notes:
452 invocations compared, always by writing raw stdout/stderr to files and using `cmp` (no shell interpolation), plus exit-status comparison: 198 named cases + a 254-case exhaustive single-byte sweep (every byte 0x01-0x7F alone, and every byte 0x01-0x7F prefixed to "7"). Baseline confirmed first: both binaries emit exactly the 24 bytes `4 5 0 0 1 2 2 3 4 4 0 2 ` (trailing space, no newline) for no-arg/1/7/10 and 0 bytes for n<=0.

Everything below matched byte-exactly in stdout, stderr, and exit status:
- NUL-adjacent patterns: literal `7\0`, `\0`, `7\0008`, empty string, `' '`.
- Unicode digits: fullwidth `１２３` and `７`, Arabic-Indic `٧`, Devanagari `७`, UTF-8 NBSP+7 (all -> atoi 0 -> 0 bytes).
- Emoji: `🎉`, `7🎉`, `🎉7`, keycap `7️⃣` (the ASCII `7` prefix is parsed by both), 2500x 🎉 (10000 bytes).
- 10000-char args: 10000 `1`s, `7`+9999 `0`s, 10000 `a`s, 10000 spaces + `7`, 9999 `0`s + `7`, 9999 newlines + `7`, `a\n` x5000, 9997 spaces + `-7`, 10000 spaces, 10000 newlines. Overflow-to-LONG_MAX-then-truncate-to--1 handled identically.
- Embedded newlines/whitespace: `\n7`, `7\n`, `7\n8`, `\n\n\n7\n\n`, `\r\n7`, `\x0b7`, `\x0c7`, ` \t\n\v\f\r7`, `\n`, `-\n7`, `7\n99999999999999999999`.
- `-0000000000000000000000005` (both 0 bytes) and `+00000000000000000000000007` (both 24 bytes), `++7`, `--7`, `+-7`, `+`, `-`, `-0`.
- Truncating-atoi edge cases: `2147483648` -> INT_MIN -> 0 bytes; `4294967297` -> 1 -> 24 bytes; `9223372036854775808` -> -1 -> 0 bytes. All identical.
- Non-numeric forms: `0x7`, `07`, `7e0`, `7.9`, `inf`, `nan`, `--`, `\`, `"7"`, `=7`.
- Extra arguments (`7 a b c \n 🎉 -1 99999`) ignored identically; argc==0 via perl exec -> both fall back to n=10 and emit the same 24 bytes.
- Locale matrix (LC_ALL=C, C.UTF-8, tr_TR.UTF-8, tr_TR.utf8, tr_TR.iso88599, de_DE.UTF-8, xx_XX.bogus, and LANG/LC_ALL/LC_CTYPE/LC_NUMERIC all unset) x 15 args: stdout byte-identical in all 120 combinations. No locale-dependent number formatting (C++ never calls std::locale::global, so the stream keeps the classic locale) and no locale-dependent isspace divergence.
- The 127-case prefix sweep confirms `c_atoi`'s hard-coded isspace set is exactly right: C++ skips only 0x09-0x0D and 0x20, matching /output/test10.rs lines 33-38, with 0 diffs.
- Dependencies: only `std` (plus crate-internal `use crate::`/`use super::`). No crates.io usage.

The sole divergence class is invalid-UTF-8 argv, reported as the two findings above (one root cause at /output/test10.rs:75, but two distinct impact classes: bytes in the parsed argument vs. bytes in arguments the C++ never reads).
